#### H.3.4 Logical Reasoning

Logical reasoning problems represent a different type of question in
MathVista. Solving these problems requires abstract thinking to deduce
the underlying patterns of numbers or shapes from figures. Current
foundation models struggle to effectively tackle logical reasoning
problems: GPT-4V achieves only 21.6% accuracy in logical reasoning,
which is a modest improvement of 8.1% over random chance, as shown in
Table
[2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts").
The challenges that logical reasoning problems present to current LMMs
are further highlighted in Figures

and

#### H.3.5 Numeric Commonsense Reasoning

Problems involving numeric commonsense reasoning on MathVista require
commonsense knowledge about daily objects and celebrities to answer
visual questions. However, these problems present significant challenges
to existing foundation models, including GPT-4V, as depicted in Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts").
For instance, Multimodal Bard struggles to understand the optical
illusion in an image (Figure
[69](#A8.F69 "Figure 69 ‣ H.3.5 Numeric Commonsense Reasoning ‣ H.3 Abilities in Mathematical Reasoning ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts"))
and to infer the age gap between two celebrities from another image
(Figure
[70](#A8.F70 "Figure 70 ‣ H.3.5 Numeric Commonsense Reasoning ‣ H.3 Abilities in Mathematical Reasoning ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")).
Figure
[71](#A8.F71 "Figure 71 ‣ H.3.5 Numeric Commonsense Reasoning ‣ H.3 Abilities in Mathematical Reasoning ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")
poses a question about the maximum volume a beaker can measure. However,
GPT-4V lacks commonsense knowledge regarding the use of a beaker,
resulting in an incorrect prediction.

### H.5 Self-Verification in GPT-4V

Self-verification is a social psychological theory asserting that people
desire others to perceive them as they see themselves. Consequently,
individuals will take active measures to ensure that others view them in
ways that confirm their stable self-concepts ([Talaifar & Swann,
2020](#bib.bib82)).

Interestingly, in our experiments, GPT-4V demonstrates an ability
similar to _self-verification_. The model can inspect its own behaviors
during the course of reasoning and can take active actions to correct
its mistakes. Note that self-verification we discuss here differs from
several recent works on improving the model’s outputs based on external
feedback ([Peng et al., 2023](#bib.bib70)) or additional generations
([Yang et al., 2023b](#bib.bib98)). The examples in Figures
[101](#A8.F101 "Figure 101 ‣ H.5 Self-Verification in GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")
and
[103](#A8.F103 "Figure 103 ‣ H.5 Self-Verification in GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")
show that GPT-4V, on its own, can inspect a set of candidate answers and
identify the one that is valid and meets all the given constraints. The
multi-step reasoning example in Figure
[102](#A8.F102 "Figure 102 ‣ H.5 Self-Verification in GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")
shows that GPT-4V can verify the validity of (the result of) each
reasoning step, and explore alternative approaches if any invalid
(intermediate) result is detected (e.g., a negative value for length).

Although self-verification does not guarantee an accurate response even
after multiple tries, especially when applying GPT-4V to visual
perception or mathematical reasoning in intricate scenarios (see Figure
[104](#A8.F104 "Figure 104 ‣ H.5 Self-Verification in GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")),
it is instrumental in improving the model performance on MathVista. We
also found that GPT-4V’s self-verification is weaker for non-English
tasks, such as Mandarin, as shown in Figure
[105](#A8.F105 "Figure 105 ‣ H.5 Self-Verification in GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts").
It is also worth noting that self-verification does not emerge in other
foundation models we studied, or at least it is not as robust as that of
GPT-4V. As shown in Figure
[106](#A8.F106 "Figure 106 ‣ H.5 Self-Verification in GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts"),
Multimodal Bard first attempts a natural language solution, followed by
a program-assisted one for verification. However, the program-aided
solution leads to a different and incorrect prediction.

The emergent ability of self-verification highlights GPT-4V’s potential
in solving rigorous reasoning and theorem-proving tasks. One of the most
exciting research topics for future work is to develop a mechanism that
allows the model to activate self-verification consistently at the right
time and to use a set of alternative approaches that maximize the
success rate of task completion.

### H.6 Self-Consistency for GPT-4V

Self-consistency ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib91)) is a decoding
strategy for chain-of-thought prompting ([Wei et al.,
2022b](#bib.bib94)). A diverse set of reasoning paths is sampled, and
the most consistent answer is selected as the final prediction. Moving
beyond vanilla greedy decoding, this method resorts to the inherent
coherence and reliability of multiple reasoning trajectories to produce
a more trustworthy conclusion. Self-consistency has been widely employed
in LLMs for complex reasoning tasks, such as math word problems and
commonsense reasoning.

In our experiments, we validated the effectiveness of using
self-consistency for GPT-4V on MathVista. Given a question and context,
we ran GPT-4V multiple times to obtain a set of different reasoning
paths and then selected the most frequent answer as the final
prediction. We found that self-consistency is instrumental in rectifying
visual perception errors (Figure
[107](#A8.F107 "Figure 107 ‣ H.6 Self-Consistency for GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")),
correcting calculation mistakes (Figure
[108](#A8.F108 "Figure 108 ‣ H.6 Self-Consistency for GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")),
and mitigating hallucinations (Figure
[109](#A8.F109 "Figure 109 ‣ H.6 Self-Consistency for GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")).
In comparison, self-consistency is less effective when GPT-4V has
difficulties in interpreting complex visual contexts (Figures
[110](#A8.F110 "Figure 110 ‣ H.6 Self-Consistency for GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts"),
[111](#A8.F111 "Figure 111 ‣ H.6 Self-Consistency for GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts"))
or extracting salient information from images (Figure
[112](#A8.F112 "Figure 112 ‣ H.6 Self-Consistency for GPT-4V ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")).

### H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction

This section investigates the use of GPT-4V for multi-turn human-AI
interaction on MathVista, as exemplified in the goal-directed dialog in
Figure
[113](#A8.F113 "Figure 113 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts").

We found that GPT-4V is effective in engaging multi-turn goal-directed
conversations with users. In particular, GPT-4V can make good use of
_hints_ (e.g., user feedback or responses) to guide the conversion to
generate desirable results. For instance, it can (1) rectify visual
perception errors based on hints (Figure
[114](#A8.F114 "Figure 114 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")),
(2) reassess reasoning steps and calculations (Figure
[115](#A8.F115 "Figure 115 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")),
(3) correct misinformation using user-provided domain-specific knowledge
(Figure
[116](#A8.F116 "Figure 116 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")),
and (4) aggregate intricate contexts over multiple turns in a human-AI
conversation (Figures
[117](#A8.F117 "Figure 117 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")
and
[118](#A8.F118 "Figure 118 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")).

We also observed failure cases in our evaluation. For instance, GPT-4V
struggles to generate correct responses when questions and user hints
are ambiguous (Figure
[119](#A8.F119 "Figure 119 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")),
or when the model fails to understand abstract shapes and concepts
visually (Figure
[120](#A8.F120 "Figure 120 ‣ H.7 GPT-4V for Multi-Turn Human-AI Interaction ‣ Appendix H A Comparative Study of GPT-4V, Bard, and Other Models ‣ MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts")).
These failures motivate the development of more powerful, conversational
foundation models.
